thread.title: When Apple ( AAPL ) released its fiscal Q1 earnings it gave,

author: J. M. Manness
title: When Apple ( AAPL ) released its fiscal Q1 earnings it gave,
text:
When Apple ( AAPL ) released its fiscal Q1 earnings it gave, as usual, its guidance for the coming quarter, including:

Revenue between $60 billion and $62 billion Even the higher figure is well below the $65.73 billion that was analyst consensus. This fact, along with the overall market downturn, was the fuel for Apple’s strong correction.

Notice how on January 1 Apple reached its peak (intraday just over $180), almost $3 over the previous high in mid December. It then began a retreat from that high. On January 26, the S&P made its high, and then fell dramatically. Apple, in turn, dropped like a stone.
In an earlier story, I discussed how Apple's “drop in unit sales” and some other negative data was not really accurate, and I presented more rational data .
Here I will address the meme that some are passing, that Apple's guidance is somehow “bad.” I will present figures and you, the investor, can decide if it is truly negative or not.
Comparison The fist thing to note is that “revenue between $60 billion and $62 billion” would represent growth over the year-ago quarter. So at a very minimum, we are looking forward to probable growth.
Let’s look at the figures. I'm including figures for both FQ1 and FQ2 (ending December and March respectively) for last year, FQ2-2016, and FQ1 this year.

Numbers are thousands for Units, and millions for Revenue. 
I have included each of the revenue figures as percentage of total revenue, and Average Selling Price (ASP) for each physical product.
Some things to note 
1 – The iPhone dominates in all quarters, but there's a significant difference between Q1 and Q2. In both years, for FQ1 the iPhone represented roughly 69.5% of revenue, while for the Q2 figures it ranged from 63% to 65% - significantly lower.
This is to be expected since the holiday quarter is heavy on higher-end gifts.
2 – The Services revenue varies inversely to the iPhone, representing a greater proportion of total revenue in the two Q2s than in the corresponding Q1s.
3 - The Services revenue continues to rise, both in terms of dollars and as percentage of total revenue. In fact last year’s Q2 was almost equal to last year’s Q1.
This also makes sense for a couple of reasons. First, typically there's a surge in App Store purchases in the holiday season as new owners purchase apps for their “new toys.” Yet many of the 77 million iPhones sold are to people who already own an iPhone that's already full of apps. Additionally, even 77 million – or that portion who are new owners - is dwarfed by the close to 1 billion existing owners who are buying other services.
The second reason is that while people may purchase a lot of apps during the holidays, as monthly payments (for iCloud and Apple Music) begin to play a larger role than apps, in overall services revenues, the spike of new owner impulse buying is smoothed out.
4 – Finally, it has been well noted that the ASP for iPhones has jumped $101 to $796 due to the higher prices of the 8 series phones and most of all the $1,000 and up iPhone X.
Calculating numbers for the current quarter If Apple is guiding to $62 billion (let’s stick with the upper figure), then if we know the percentage spread for each product category, then we can easily calculate the other numbers.
The argument has been made that FQ2 will be much higher this year since the iPhone X was available so late in the season then sales will carry over into Q2. While the number of unit sales is not as high as this argument was originally projecting, still the overall line of reasoning makes some sense. It is likely that we will see some degree of delayed sales of the iPhone X showing up in the current quarter.
So, to calculate sales numbers, we need to make some assumptions.
Assumption #1 
Apple will make (or even beat) its high-end guidance.
I think there are definitely headwinds, and the X has not performed quite as well as Tim Cook, or investors, would have liked. Just today there are more reports on iPhone X OLED cuts at Samsung ( OTC:SSNLF ) . Yet I think the uncertainty has led Cook to be a bit more conservative on the guidance than in the recent past. So I believe that (barring any economic catastrophe) Apple will make the high-end number.
Assumption #2 
This will likely boost iPhone revenue as a percentage of sales, although not as high as the almost 70% of the last quarter. I have chosen 66% as a likely figure. This is significantly higher than last year’s figure.
Assumption #3 
The next point is the ASP. I think this is likely to stay near the current figure as the iPhone X is likely to play a large role in sales. In spite of the negativity, we should remember it has been the best-selling smartphone worldwide since its release.
Assumption #4 
The other products are likely to proportion out similarly to the previous Q2, except that Services will likely continue to rise allowing for the increase in iPhone's proportion.

If we have a prediction of total revenue, we can then complete the revenue and unit numbers. In the table below, I have both Apple’s high-end quarter, and a slightly more optimistic figure that I dub My Projection .

Results 
It is important to note several things.
1 – The most important thing is that in spite of the fact that analysts are disappointed with Apple’s guidance, at the upper figure there's over 17% revenue growth . This is hardly worth crying over.
2 - Even at Apple’s $62 billion level for overall revenue, and a high ASP, the product line shows 1.4% growth in units and 23% in revenue. If the ASP were to fall, even slightly, then units growth would be even higher.
3 – The chart depends heavily on the iPhone as 66% total revenue. This seems rational given assumption No. 2 noted above. However, it is still speculative. A downward deviation from this would mean iPhone unit sales would be slipping.
Summary The market often focuses on the negatives in Apple reports. If we look at things realistically, then we see that the numbers are a lot more positive than at first glance.
Certainly, it appears that a great surge of purchases for the new model X has not occurred, but they have not been shabby either. It still leads the weekly sales lists.
Regarding the projections, if sales go to the high end of guidance, then growth will be a significant 17% overall, and iPhone sales would show modest growth.
If iPhone sales do really slip, then I think it would cause a significant drop in overall revenue. Services and Other Products are gaining in importance, but we cannot expect miracles there.
A modest beat on revenue would be driven by even higher sales.
I think we should keep in mind what Apple has done here. Something that's really extraordinary. In face of slowing unit growth , Apple has managed to grow revenue by making an even higher end, more expensive smartphone. And they have succeeded in it! The enormous jump in ASP last quarter cannot be denied. Your comments are appreciated.
